title.en: Codes for letters using binary representation

summary.en: Children turn letters into numbers, and numbers into on and off cards, to send a secret message.

en: See that computers store letters as numbers.
Use five cards (1, 2, 4, 8, 16 dots) to make a number.
Send and read a short coded word.
Five dot cards: 16, 8, 4, 2, 1
An alphabet strip (A = 1, B = 2, and so on)
Paper and pencil
Ask: how does a computer know which letter to show? Count the letters of the alphabet together.
Explain that A is 1, B is 2, C is 3, and so on.
Put the five cards in a row, biggest on the left (16, 8, 4, 2, 1).
Say a pattern such as No, Yes, No, No, No. The cards with Yes are on. Add the dots: that is 8, which is the letter H.
Say No, Yes, No, No, Yes. That is 9, the letter I. Together they spell HI.
Let the children choose a short word, work out its codes, and send it to a partner who decodes it.
Why do we need a fifth card?
Could we use other words than yes and no, like up and down?
What other things on a keyboard need a code?

grown_up_note.en: Print an alphabet strip with numbers to help children who are still learning the order of letters. Start with two or three letters and build up.

summary.en: Children colour grids using rows of 0s and 1s, and learn that a computer stores a picture as numbers.

en: Know that screen pictures are made of tiny squares called pixels.
Decode a row of numbers into black and white squares.
Understand that a picture can be stored as a list of numbers.
Printed colour-by-number grids where 1 means black and 0 means white
Black pencils or felt tips
Spare copies for mistakes
Explain that screens are made of tiny squares called pixels (short for picture elements).
Show a simple black and white picture. Each pixel is either black or white, so a computer only needs to remember which.
Hand out a small grid. Each row has numbers. Colour a square black for 1 and leave it white for 0.
Colour row by row. A picture should appear. Check with a neighbour.
Try a bigger picture in a group, with each child doing some rows.
Discuss: how did the numbers tell you the picture?
What would happen if one number were wrong?
How many numbers do you need for a bigger picture?
How could we show colours instead of black and white?

grown_up_note.en: A megapixel camera has a million pixels. Pencil is easier than pen because children can rub out mistakes. Look at the original lesson page for the printable pictures.

summary.en: With cards in order from smallest to biggest, children find a number in only a few guesses.

en: Know that sorted lists are quicker to search.
Use the middle card to throw away half the cards at once.
Compare with searching an unsorted list.
15 cards in order from lowest to highest, numbers between 1 and 100, animal side up
A target number such as 52
Lay out the 15 cards in order. Tell the children the numbers go from small to large.
Ask them to find 52 by turning over as few cards as possible.
Start in the middle. If the number is too small, the card you want is to the right. If too big, to the left.
Throw away half the cards and look at the middle of what is left.
Count the guesses with the class. It is only a few.
Try other targets. Compare with last time, when the cards were not in order.
Why does sorting help?
What would you do with 100 cards?
What if the number is not in the list?

grown_up_note.en: Avoid using numbers 1 to 15 in order, since children will just count along. Spread the numbers out.

summary.en: Groups invent their own picture 'programming language' of exercises and then program a friend to follow it.

en: See that a programming language is a set of commands someone designed.
Make picture cards that stand for actions.
Put commands in order to make a program.
Plain cards or paper and felt tips
A hula hoop and whiteboards (optional)
Space to exercise safely
Talk about who makes programming languages. Today the class will design its own fitness language.
As a class, list exercises: running on the spot, star jumps, catching a bean bag.
In groups of three, draw a GO card, four exercise cards and a finishing pose card.
Lay the cards in a row with GO first and the finishing pose last.
Groups walk round and try to work out what the other groups' cards mean. Some will be easy and some will need to be learned.
Join back together: this is like real programming languages, where some things look familiar and others must be learned.
Run a program: a group lays out cards and a friend does each exercise in order.
Which cards were easy to understand?
What would you add to your language?
What happens if the cards are in a different order?

grown_up_note.en: Keep activities gentle and safe. The learning is about commands and order, not about how fast the exercise is.

summary.en: Children pretend to be tiny switches inside a computer. Cards with dots can be turned over, and together they show numbers.

en: Understand that a computer uses things that are either on or off.
Count with cards of 1, 2, 4 and 8 dots.
Notice that each card has double the dots of the one before.
Four cards with 1, 2, 4 and 8 dots (draw them on paper)
Four volunteers
A clear space to stand in a line
Tell the children a computer is full of tiny things that can be on or off, like a light switch. One of these is called a bit.
Pick four children to be bits. Stand them in a row. Give the 1-dot card to the child on the right.
Give the next child the 2-dot card. Ask: how many dots will the next card have? Let them guess without telling them they are wrong.
Hand out the 4-dot and 8-dot cards. Talk about the pattern: each card has double the dots of the one before.
Each bit can show its card or hide it (turn it over). Call out a number from 0 to 15 and let the bits show or hide cards to make it. Add up the dots you can see.
Swap places so everyone gets a turn being a different bit.
What number do you get if every card is hidden?
What is the biggest number the four cards can make?
Where else do we see things that are just on or off?

grown_up_note.en: Do not correct wrong guesses straight away. Keep going so the children discover the pattern. Counting dots one by one is fine.

summary.en: Children search for a hidden number one card at a time and count how many guesses it takes.

en: Understand searching means looking for one thing in a list.
Predict and count the number of guesses.
See that luck changes how many guesses you need.
15 cards with an animal on one side and a hidden number on the other, in no order
Sticky notes
A line on the board for predictions
Ask: you lent a book to a friend and forgot who. You visit six houses. How many visits will you need?
Each child writes a guess on a sticky note and puts it on a line from 1 to 6.
Lay out 15 cards animal-side up. The numbers underneath are in no order.
Pick a target number. A child turns over cards one at a time until they find it, while the class counts.
Try again with different targets. Write the number of guesses each time.
Look at the results. Was it ever the first card? The last?
Is it ever fast to search when nothing is in order?
What is the most guesses you could need?
How could we make searching faster?

grown_up_note.en: Change the numbers to match what the children are learning. It is good if the numbers are not neatly spread out.

title.en: Investigating variations using the Sorting Network

summary.en: Children try the sorting network with repeated numbers and with things that are not numbers, like heights.

en: Predict what a program will do before running it.
See that the network still works when two cards are the same.
Sort things other than numbers.
The chalk sorting network from the first lesson
Number cards with two the same, for example 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5
Other things to sort: heights, colours, sizes
Remind the class how the network works: meet in a box, smaller to the left, bigger to the right.
Variation 1: use cards where two numbers are the same. Ask what happens when two equal cards meet. (It does not matter who goes where.)
Ask the class to predict the ending, then run it. The equal cards end up next to each other.
Variation 2: ask what else we could sort. Try heights, colours, or sizes.
Run the network with one of those and check the result.
Talk about what stayed the same each time.
Did you guess right?
What can you sort besides numbers?
Why does the network still work?

grown_up_note.en: Do the first sorting network lesson first. Letting children predict is the key part.

summary.en: A card trick that shows how a computer can find a mistake and fix it by adding one extra row and one extra column.

en: Know that computers can notice when data changes by mistake.
Count and add cards in rows and columns.
Use the trick to find a flipped card.
36 two-sided cards (for example black on one side and white on the other)
A table or whiteboard
A helper
Tell the class you have a magic trick. Ask a helper to lay out a 5 by 5 square of cards, some black and some white, in any pattern.
Say you will add one more row and one more column. Add cards so that every row and every column has an even number of black cards.
Now you have a 6 by 6 square. Ask the class to close their eyes while the helper flips exactly one card.
Look at each row and column. Find the row that has an odd number of black cards, and the column that has an odd number.
The card where that row and column cross is the one that was flipped. Flip it back.
Let pairs try the trick on their own.
Why does the trick always work?
Where might a computer need to find mistakes, like a scratched disc or a QR code?

grown_up_note.en: Practise the trick yourself first. Children enjoy a bit of magic patter. The aim is the idea that extra information lets a computer check itself.

title.en: Reinforcing numeracy through a Sorting Network

summary.en: Six children walk through a chalk network, comparing numbers at each box, until they end up in order.

en: Compare two numbers and say which is smaller.
Follow a step-by-step set of rules.
See how six people can finish the job sooner than one.
A network of circles, lines and boxes drawn with chalk or tape
Six number cards (1 to 6)
Six children per turn
Draw the network on the ground. Six circles at the start, lines that lead into boxes, six circles at the end.
Give six children one number card each, in a mixed-up order, and let them stand at the start.
Two children follow their lines until they meet at a box. They say hello and show their cards.
The child with the smaller number leaves by the left line. The bigger leaves by the right.
Everyone keeps following lines and meeting in boxes until they reach the end.
Look: are they in order? Try again with new cards.
Which jobs go faster if more people help?
Which do not?
Did you need to know all the numbers to take part?

grown_up_note.en: Only one team uses the network at a time while others watch. Later try fractions, bigger numbers or other things to sort.

title.en: Reinforcing sequencing in binary number systems

summary.en: Small groups make up a short play that counts in binary using two opposite things instead of dot cards.

en: Show on and off with any two opposite things.
Count from 0 up to 8 or more using four 'bits'.
Take turns being each bit.
Anything with two states: hats on or off, loud or quiet sounds, two kinds of counters
Groups of four children
A phone or camera (optional)
Talk about opposites: hot and cold, up and down, happy and sad. A computer uses on and off in the same way.
In groups of four, choose how to show on and off. It must not be the dot cards.
Each child picks one bit: 8, 4, 2 or 1. Line up from the biggest to the smallest.
Practise counting from 1 to 8 together. Each bit turns on or off at the right moment.
Swap roles so everyone has been each bit.
Each group shows their play and the class works out the number they are showing.
What did your group use for on and off?
Which bit changed the most often?
Which number was hardest to show?

grown_up_note.en: If a group has extra children, they can film the play or be the audience that guesses the number.

summary.en: Children act as programmer, tester and robot on a floor grid, and learn why clear step-by-step instructions matter.

en: Write a simple program with arrow commands.
Find and fix mistakes (debugging).
Understand that a robot only does what its instructions say.
A grid on the floor (chalk, masking tape or a chessboard pattern)
Arrow cards or paper: forward, turn left, turn right
An object to rescue
Make a floor grid and put an object to rescue on one square.
Choose three roles: the Developer who writes the program, the Tester who reads it out, and the Bot who follows it.
Decide the commands: an arrow for forward, and left and right turns.
The Developer writes the whole program first. The Bot cannot be steered while it walks.
The Tester reads the commands one at a time and the Bot moves. Does the Bot reach the object?
If not, find the bug together and fix the program. Debugging is part of the fun.
Swap roles and try a new rescue.
Why must instructions be very clear?
When did you get unclear instructions in real life?
What was the bug and how did you fix it?

grown_up_note.en: The teacher can play the Developer first to show the idea. Praise finding bugs, not just getting it right the first time.

summary.en: Children shrink a picture by writing how many squares in a row are the same, a trick called run-length encoding.

en: Understand that computers try to store pictures using less space.
Count runs of the same colour in a row.
Rebuild a picture from a short code.
Grid paper or printed 8 by 8 grids
Black and white pencils
A whiteboard
Show an 8 by 8 picture made of black and white squares. Ask how you could describe it without naming every square.
Teach the trick: instead of naming each square, count how many of the same colour come in a row.
Do the first row together. Start with white. For example, 3 white then 2 black then 3 white becomes 3, 2, 3.
Let children write the code for the other rows.
Swap codes with a partner. Each partner colours the picture back from the code.
Compare: did the code use fewer numbers than the 64 squares?
Which pictures squeeze well, and which do not?
Why do computers want to use less space?
Where have you seen pictures that were sent or saved?

grown_up_note.en: Always start with white so the code is clear. This idea is part of how pictures get small enough to send in messages.

title.en: Codes for letters using binary representation

summary.en: Children write secret messages by turning letters into numbers and numbers into patterns of on and off.

en: Show that letters can be stored as numbers.
Convert a letter to a binary pattern with five bits.
Send and decode a short message.
Five dot cards: 16, 8, 4, 2, 1
An alphabet chart (A = 1, B = 2, ...)
Paper and pencils
Ask how a computer knows which letter to show. Number the alphabet from 1 to 26.
Work out the code for one letter together, for example D is 4, which needs the 4 card on and the others off: OFF OFF ON OFF OFF.
Write the code for your name or a short word, one letter at a time.
Swap messages with a partner. Decode each other's patterns back into letters.
Discuss what a computer must also store: capital letters, digits and punctuation, and letters of other languages.
Why do we need five bits for 26 letters?
What else would a computer need codes for?
How could you send your code to someone far away?

grown_up_note.en: If your alphabet has extra letters or accents, talk about how a code would need more bits. Real computers use a bigger standard code.

summary.en: With the cards in order, children find a number in just a few guesses by always checking the middle.

en: Use the order of a list to search faster.
Explain binary search in their own words.
Compare with searching an unsorted list.
15 cards sorted from lowest to highest (spread between 1 and 100)
A target number such as 52
Lay out sorted cards face down. Say they run from small to large.
Ask the class to find 52 using as few turned cards as possible.
Turn over the middle card. If it is too big, throw away the right half. If too small, throw away the left half.
Look at the middle of what is left and repeat until you find 52.
Count the guesses with the class. Try other targets.
Compare with the unsorted search. What changed?
How many guesses at most for 15 cards?
What if we doubled the cards?
What if the number is not there?

grown_up_note.en: This method is called binary search. Do not use 1 to 15 in order, or children will just count along.

summary.en: Children use cards with 1, 2, 4 and 8 dots as 'bits' to make any number from 0 to 15, and see how a computer counts using only on and off.

en: Explain how binary digits (bits) represent numbers.
Make numbers from 0 to 15 with four cards.
Spot the doubling pattern and count in binary.
Cards with 1, 2, 4 and 8 dots (a fifth card with 16 dots for later)
Four volunteers
Paper to record results
Ask: how does a digital device store information? Write down every answer, then come back to them at the end.
Four children stand in a line and hold the cards 8, 4, 2, 1 from left to right, with the dots hidden at first.
Reveal the pattern: each card has twice as many dots as the one to its right.
A card is either shown (on, 1) or hidden (off, 0). Call out a number and let the line show the right cards. Add the dots to check.
Count from 0 to 15 by changing as few cards as possible each time. Write the pattern of ones and zeros on the board.
Add a fifth card. What is the biggest number now?
What is the biggest number with four cards? With five?
Why does a computer use on and off?
Which card changes most often when counting?

grown_up_note.en: Resist the urge to correct guesses. Let the children find the doubling rule themselves. Real computers have billions of bits.

summary.en: Children search for a hidden number one card at a time and discover how many guesses it takes when the list is in no order.

en: Define searching and a search algorithm.
Predict, count and graph the number of guesses.
Understand why unsorted lists take longer.
15 cards with a hidden number on the back, in no order
Sticky notes
A line or graph on the board
Ask how many house visits you would need to find a lent book among six houses. Everyone puts a prediction on a line.
Lay out the cards face down with a picture up. The numbers underneath are not in order.
Choose a target number. One child turns cards over until they find it. The class counts the guesses.
Repeat with other targets and record each count.
Look at the spread: sometimes lucky, sometimes the last card. On average, about half the cards.
Discuss how the number of guesses grows as the list gets bigger.
Was it ever one guess? Was it ever all of them?
What if there were a million cards?
Could sorting the cards help?

grown_up_note.en: Try different numbers so children cannot guess where the target is. Keep a class tally.

title.en: Investigating variations using the Sorting Network

summary.en: Children test the sorting network with repeated numbers and with other things to sort, and predict what will happen.

en: Predict an outcome before testing it.
Explain why the network works even with repeated values.
Sort things other than numbers.
The sorting network from the first lesson
Cards with repeated numbers
Things to sort: heights, colours, sizes, words
Recap how the network works.
Use cards where two values are equal. Ask what happens when equal cards meet.
Predict, then run the network. Equal cards end up next to each other.
Choose something new to sort, like heights or the alphabet. Decide what 'smaller' means for it.
Run the network with the new cards and check the result.
Discuss what stays the same each time and why.
Did your prediction match?
What else could you sort?
What if the rule for smaller changed?

grown_up_note.en: Complete the first sorting network lesson first. Prediction is the heart of this lesson.

summary.en: A card trick shows how a computer adds one extra row and column so it can find and fix a single mistake.

en: Explain why computers need to check data for errors.
Make every row and column have an even number of black cards.
Find a flipped card using the odd row and odd column.
36 two-sided cards (black and white)
Pairs of children, each with their own set
A whiteboard or table
Ask: have you ever had a disc or QR code that would not work? Computers often correct such mistakes automatically.
Lay out a 5 by 5 square of black and white cards with no pattern.
Add a sixth row and a sixth column so every row and every column has an even number of black cards. (This extra card is called a parity bit.)
While everyone looks away, flip exactly one card.
Find the one row and the one column that now have an odd number of black cards. The card where they cross is the flipped one.
Pairs practise. Then try flipping two cards. What happens?
Why does the trick work?
What happens if two cards flip?
Where do computers use this idea?

grown_up_note.en: Practise first so you can do the trick smoothly. Real systems use much better versions, but the idea is the same.

summary.en: Children use a short recipe of adding and multiplying to find the last digit of a barcode, which is how scanners notice mistakes.

en: Know that barcodes include a check digit.
Follow a step-by-step recipe (an algorithm).
Detect a mistake in a barcode.
Real barcodes from products (12 or 13 digits)
Paper, pencil and a calculator if needed
A whiteboard
Ask: do you check your receipt at the shop? Barcodes are so reliable that we trust them.
Take a 13-digit barcode and cover the last digit.
Write the 12 digits in two rows: the 1st, 3rd, 5th... digits on top and the 2nd, 4th, 6th... on the bottom.
Add up the top row. Add up the bottom row and multiply that total by 3. Add the two results together.
Take the last digit of that sum. The check digit is what you need to add to reach the next multiple of ten.
Compare with the covered digit. Then change one digit and see that the check fails.
Why is the last digit useful?
What if two digits swap places?
Where else do check digits appear, like library books or bank cards?

grown_up_note.en: This is an arithmetic-heavy lesson, so let children use a calculator if they like. The modulo lesson is a good lead-in.

title.en: Reinforcing numeracy through a Sorting Network

summary.en: Six children walk through a chalk network and compare numbers at each box until they come out in order.

en: Compare numbers and put them in order.
Follow a fixed algorithm.
See how teamwork lets many steps happen at once.
A sorting network drawn on the ground
Number cards (whole numbers, then bigger numbers, fractions or decimals)
Six children per turn
Ask for jobs that finish sooner with more helpers, and jobs that do not.
Draw the network: six start circles, lines meeting in boxes, six end circles.
Six children start at the circles holding mixed-up number cards.
Two children meet in a box, say hello and compare. The smaller number goes left, the bigger goes right.
Everyone follows the lines and meets in more boxes until they reach the end.
Check: are they in order? Run it again with new cards.
Which steps could happen at the same time?
Does it work with any six numbers?
How would you sort twenty?

grown_up_note.en: Use bigger numbers, decimals or fractions for a challenge.

title.en: Reinforcing sequencing in binary number systems

summary.en: Groups invent a play that counts in binary using any two opposite things, then perform it for the class.

en: Show on and off with different objects, sounds or actions.
Order four bits from biggest to smallest and count to 15.
Explain the pattern to someone else.
Anything with two states (hats, sounds, lights, counters)
Groups of four
Optional camera or phone
Brainstorm opposites together. A computer uses on and off in the same way.
In groups of four, pick how to show on and off and decide who is the 8, 4, 2 and 1 bit.
Practise counting up from 0, with each person switching at the right time.
Swap roles so everyone is each bit once.
Perform: the audience calls a number and the group shows it. Others work out which number it is.
Which bit moved the most when counting?
Which idea did you like best from another group?
Could you show a number bigger than 15?

grown_up_note.en: Extra children can film the plays or be the audience. Be open to unusual ideas.

summary.en: Children program a 'rocket' to cross a floor grid, using clear instructions and debugging with three roles.

en: Write a program as a list of clear steps.
Test and debug a program.
Explain why computers need exact instructions.
A grid on the floor (chalk or tape)
Arrow cards or paper
A target square to mark 'Mars'
Ask: why is it important to give very clear instructions? Share a time when instructions were unclear.
Make a grid and mark the target. One child is the rocket (the Bot), one is the Programmer, one is the Tester.
Agree on the commands: arrows for forward, turn left, turn right.
The Programmer writes the whole program first. The Bot cannot be steered halfway.
The Tester reads the program out. The Bot follows it. Did the rocket reach Mars?
Debug: find what went wrong and change the program. Swap roles and try a harder route.
What was the hardest bug to find?
Why not just steer the rocket step by step?
What instructions would a real rocket need?

grown_up_note.en: Show the idea yourself first by being the Programmer. Celebrate bugs found.

summary.en: Pairs play the same hunt game, but this time the numbers are in order, and they discover binary search.

en: Use the order of the list to cut the search short.
Describe binary search.
Compare with the unsorted game.
Sorted Number Hunt sheets (printable on the original lesson page)
Pencils
A class chart
Ask: is it easier to find a book in a library if the books are in alphabetical order?
Pairs sit back to back with a sheet of 31 sorted boxes.
One partner picks a number that the other must find. Guess the middle box first.
After each guess, the partner says higher or lower. Discard half the boxes every time.
Count guesses and add them to the class chart.
Compare this chart with the unsorted one.
How many guesses did it take at most?
Why is guessing the middle smart?
Could this work for billions of items?

grown_up_note.en: This method is called binary search. It can search huge lists with only a handful of guesses.

summary.en: Pairs play a guessing game on a sheet of 31 hidden numbers that are in no order, and count how many guesses they need.

en: Search an unsorted list.
Count and record guesses.
See why unsorted data is slow to search.
The Number Hunt sheets (printable on the original lesson page)
Pencils
A class chart to record guesses
Ask how you would find a book on a shelf if the books are in no order.
Put children in pairs, back to back. Each has a sheet of 31 boxes.
One partner picks a number that the other must find by guessing boxes one at a time.
Count how many guesses it takes. Write it on the class chart or spreadsheet.
Swap roles and play again.
Look at the chart together. What do you notice?
What is the fewest guesses? The most?
Is there a smarter way to guess?
What would help?

grown_up_note.en: Have other games ready for children who finish early, since some searches take many guesses.

summary.en: Children explore 'clock arithmetic' and remainders, a calculation that computers use all the time.

en: Understand that counting can wrap around, like the hours on a clock.
Find a remainder after dividing.
Know why computers use the modulo operator.
A clock face with only 10 points (0 to 9)
Paper and pencils
Counters
Ask: what month comes after December? What day is 4 days before Friday?
If you park at 5pm for 8 hours, when does the ticket run out? Add 8 to 17 and wrap around the 24-hour clock.
Show a clock with only ten positions. Start at 0, add numbers and say where you land.
Connect to remainders: 23 divided by 10 leaves 3, which is the same as where you land after going round the ten-point clock.
Practise with different clock sizes and numbers.
Discuss where wrapping around is useful, like repeating patterns, turns and angles.
What does going round the clock have to do with remainders?
Where do you meet wrap-around in everyday life?
What would a clock with 7 points look like?

grown_up_note.en: This lesson is mostly maths. It prepares for the barcode and error-checking lessons.

summary.en: Children walk through a large tree drawn on the ground, turning over nodes, and learn how a binary search tree stores things so they are quick to find.

en: Describe a binary search tree.
Search a tree by going left or right.
Compare it with searching a sorted list.
A big tree drawn on the ground with chalk or tape
Large cards or plates with a number hidden underneath
Space outside or in a hall
Remind the class how binary search works on a sorted list.
Show the tree: lines to follow and nodes with hidden numbers underneath.
Pick a target. The child starts at the top node and turns it over.
If the target is smaller, go left. If it is bigger, go right. Repeat until you find it.
Let children arrange new numbers into their own tree shapes.
Compare how many nodes you visit with searching a list.
Does the shape of the tree change the search?
How is this different from binary search on a list?
Where could a computer use a tree?

grown_up_note.en: Children often mix up binary search and binary search trees. They share a half-at-a-time idea, but they are different. This is the most advanced lesson in the set.
